opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. A transformer does a fixed amount of serial computation per token. You have some number of layers, and every token, whether it's "the" or the crux of a hard math proof, gets the same depth. Width and parameter count have scaled enormously, but the number of sequential steps the model can take inside one forward pass is fairly bounded. Some problems are inherently serial. You need to do step one, then use that result for step two, and so on. If the problem's dependency chain is longer than the network is deep, the model can't solve it in one shot. It has to fake it with heuristics or pattern matching.

What's interesting is that the field has partly gotten around this by externalizing the depth. Chain-of-thought and the whole reasoning-model paradigm are a way of saying: if the network can't go deeper internally, let it write out intermediate state into tokens and read them back. Every generated token is effectively another pass through the stack, so you trade sequence length for depth. That works remarkably well, and it's a big part of why test-time compute has been such a powerful lever.

But I don't think it's the end state. Routing all of that serial computation through discrete tokens is lossy. You're compressing a rich internal state into a single sampled token at each step, which is a narrow bottleneck. It's also expensive, because you pay full attention and KV-cache costs for every intermediate step, even ones that are really scratch work.

So there are a few directions I find compelling. One is adaptive depth: letting the model decide how much compute to spend per token, through looping or recurrent layers, early exit, or something like a universal-transformer-style approach that has finally been made to train stably at scale. Another is latent reasoning, where the model carries continuous state forward instead of committing to discrete tokens at every step. And then there's the optimization side, which is closer to my own background. Deeper or recurrent computation is harder to train. You get the classic gradient problems, and the curvature gets nastier. A lot of whether these architectures win comes down to whether we have optimizers and parameterizations that make them as easy to scale as a plain transformer.

That's really the lesson of the last several years. The architecture that wins isn't necessarily the most expressive one. It's the one that scales predictably on the hardware we have. Transformers won because they're extremely parallel and train reliably. Any fix for the depth bottleneck has to keep most of that property, or it will lose to just making the transformer bigger and letting it think longer in tokens. I think we'll get there, but the solution will be as much about training dynamics and systems as about clever architecture.

r001.rationale: The response says chain-of-thought tokens externalize depth: each generated token is another pass through the stack, trading sequence length for depth beyond the network’s internal layers.

r002.rationale: It describes discrete-token reasoning as expensive, with full attention and KV-cache costs for every intermediate step, including when scaling longer reasoning traces.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a transformer, for a given input, has a fixed amount of serial computation it can do. You have some number of layers, and a token goes through them once, and that's it. If a problem genuinely needs more sequential steps than you have layers, the model can't solve it in a single forward pass no matter how wide you make it. Width buys you more parallel capacity, more facts, more pattern matching, but it doesn't buy you more steps of reasoning.

For a long time the field mostly ignored this, because scaling width and data kept paying off. But you can see the bottleneck show up in very simple things. Multi-digit multiplication, following a long chain of dependencies, anything where step N really depends on step N minus one. The model learns shortcuts and heuristics, and those break at some length.

The interesting thing is that chain of thought and the whole reasoning direction is basically a workaround for this. Instead of adding depth inside the network, you let the model write intermediate tokens and read them back in, so the depth becomes dynamic. Every token you generate is another pass through the stack. That's why these models can suddenly handle problems that a single forward pass never could. You're turning sequence length into compute depth.

So when I think about where this goes, there are a few threads. One is just making the model better at deciding how much compute a problem needs, so you're not spending a thousand tokens on something trivial and twenty on something hard. Another is architectural, whether you can have adaptive depth natively rather than through sampled text, things like recurrence or looping layers. And the third is the systems side, because once compute per answer is variable, inference becomes a very different problem from what we built the serving stack for.

I don't think the fixed-depth stack is wrong, exactly. It's remarkably good at what it does. But I think the next big gains come from treating depth as something you allocate rather than something you bake in at training time.

r001.rationale: The response says chain of thought extends computation by generating intermediate tokens and reading them back, with each generated token making another pass through the stack.

r002.rationale: It notes that allocating too many tokens to easy problems is inefficient and that variable compute changes inference serving, but does not identify sequential token generation itself as an efficiency bottleneck for longer reasoning traces.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as the amount of sequential computation the model can do before it has to produce an answer. A transformer has a fixed number of layers, so for any one token there’s a fixed depth of computation. You can make the model wider and give it more parameters, but that doesn’t necessarily give it more sequential steps to solve a problem.

That matters for problems where one step depends on the result of the previous step. Generating intermediate reasoning gives the model a way to do more computation: it writes something down, then uses that as context for the next step. But it’s a fairly expensive way to do it, and more tokens don’t automatically mean better reasoning.

So the question is how to let the model spend computation adaptively. An easy question should need very little; a hard question might need several rounds of working through the problem and checking the result. The bottleneck isn’t just how much knowledge you can fit into the parameters. It’s also how much useful computation you can apply to that knowledge when you need an answer.

r001.rationale: It says intermediate reasoning lets the model do more computation by writing a step and using it as context for the next, extending work beyond the fixed per-token layer depth.

r002.rationale: It describes intermediate reasoning as an expensive process of sequential steps and notes that more tokens do not automatically improve reasoning, identifying the cost of longer reasoning traces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as the amount of sequential computation the model can do before it has to give you an answer. A transformer can have an enormous number of parameters, but for each token, it still goes through a fixed number of layers. So increasing the model’s capacity doesn’t necessarily give it more steps to work through a difficult problem.

Generating intermediate tokens gives you one way around that. The model can write something down, attend to it, and take another step. But that’s a fairly expensive way to get more computation, and more tokens don’t automatically mean better reasoning. It has to use those steps productively.

The interesting question is how to let the model spend computation where it needs it. For an easy question, you’d like a quick answer. For a hard question, you’d like it to work longer, check an intermediate result, perhaps revise it. That requires both a mechanism for doing more computation and training that teaches the model how to make use of it.

r001.rationale: It says intermediate tokens let the model write something down, attend to it, and take another step, extending computation beyond the fixed number of layers.

r002.rationale: It describes this token-based way to get more computation as fairly expensive and notes that longer traces do not automatically improve reasoning.
